newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina plans austerity for IMF deficit target.
newsitem.headline: Argentina plans austerity for IMF deficit target.

text.p: Argentina has drawn up a new package of spending and revenue measures to keep it to an IMF-agreed 1997 budget deficit of $4.5 billion, according to the text of a letter of intent.

The letter of intent with the International Monetary Fund for a three-year Extended Fund Facility loan to take over from a stand-by accord ending this year was agreed on in December and announced by Economy Minister Roque Fernandez Tuesday.

The text released late Thursday talks of a 1997 deficit of $3.0 billion, or one percent of gross domestic product, versus $6.0 billion seen for 1996. But it acknowledges that the cost of transferring pensions from provinces to the central government and of state layoffs will push the deficit up to $4.5 billion.

It fixes cumulative quarterly deficit targets, not including pension transfer and layoff costs, of $1.04 billion in the first quarter, rising to $1.4 billion by the end of the second quarter and mounting to $2.0 billion by the completion of the third quarter.

Including the pension transfer and layoff costs, the cumulative quarter targets are: $1.64 billion for the first quarter rising to $2.3 billion by the end of the second quarter and climbing to $3.2 billion by the completion of the third quarter.

Fernandez submitted a 1997 budget to Congress meeting the above targets, but since the legislators pushed the deficit up to $3.4 billion, "the government has elaborated a new package of revenue and cost-cutting measures" to reach the IMF target.

That includes $285 million of discretional spending cuts together with tax measures to raise $190 million including the already-announced decision to hike value-added tax on consumer loans back up to 21 percent from 10.5 percent and plans to put income tax on export reimbursements.
The accord foresees GDP growth of about 5.0 percent this year and consumer inflation of 1.0 percent.

There is also a commitment to the unpopular labor reforms President Carlos Menem ruled by decree last month -- since condemned as "unconstitutional" by one judge and suspended by another pending a full explanation by the government.
